vignette:
Meera had always prided herself on her composure. For forty years, she had been a pilot, a woman who commanded passenger jets, who calmly navigated thunderstorms and crosswinds, and who was trusted with hundreds of lives at a time. Now, at seventy-nine, she felt she couldn't trust herself to get through a single night. The trouble began a month ago, when her husband, Sameer, was hospitalized for a severe bout of pneumonia. For the first time in fifty-four years of marriage, Meera was sleeping alone. The vast emptiness of their king-sized bed felt cavernous and threatening. Each night, she would delay the inevitable, watching old movies until her eyes burned, finally climbing into bed well after 2 a.m., only to lie there, rigid and alert. Every creak of their high-rise apartment building, every siren in the distant Chicago streets, was a source of alarm. Several times a night, she would startle awake, heart hammering, convinced someone was at the door, and would have to get up to check the deadbolt she knew she had already secured.

The daily visits to the hospital were their own form of torture. The moment the elevator doors opened onto Sameer's floor, the sharp, antiseptic smell would hit her, and she would be a child again. It wasn't a thought or a simple memory; it was a complete sensory hijacking. Suddenly, the hospital corridor's polished linoleum would feel like the cold floor of her childhood home in the dead of night. The memory of the event that haunted her never arrived as a clear narrative, but in jagged, disconnected pieces: the smell of Dettol her mother would use to clean a split lip, the muffled thud against a wall from her parents' bedroom, her father's voice, low and menacing. These fragments felt more real, more vivid and present, than the memory of what she had eaten for breakfast. She would feel the same childhood terror rise in her chest, a feeling so immediate it was as if the frightening event was happening right now, in the sterile hospital hallway.

Back in the quiet of her apartment, the feelings would linger. She would snap at a well-meaning neighbor who asked about Sameer, the irritability a raw, exposed nerve. To manage the distress, she would find herself in the kitchen, eating an entire sleeve of crackers or a pint of ice cream, the physical fullness a temporary balm for the emotional void. Some nights, when sleep was impossible, she would lie in the dark and construct elaborate revenge fantasies. In them, she wasn't a small, helpless girl, but the capable pilot she had become, striding back in time to confront her father, protecting her mother with a strength she had never possessed as a child. The fantasies brought a fleeting sense of power, but it always evaporated by morning, leaving behind only shame.

The dissonance between her past self and her present reality was agonizing. The woman who had navigated the globe couldn't deal with even the slightest upset. She had come to believe that her reactions proved she was a lousy coper, that she couldn't rely on herself for even the most basic sense of security. The very foundation of her identity-her competence, her steadiness-felt like a lie. Even a simple thing, like the classical Indian music she and Sameer used to enjoy, was now a minefield. A certain raga came on the radio one afternoon, the same one that had been playing softly during one of the worst nights of her childhood, and she was instantly overwhelmed by a wave of panic so intense she had to flee her own living room. Sameer is due to be discharged next week, and this is what finally propelled Meera to seek help. Her greatest fear is not that the memories will stay, but that this fragile, hypervigilant, and angry version of herself is who she is now, and that the man she loves will come home not to the strong partner he has always known, but to a frightened stranger.
